About the Author

I am Sukesh Marla, a developer just like you. Let me quickly and in very short tell you about my journey to this book.

Programmer

I started my career in 2008 as a .net developer with a company called Pi Techniques. It was an excellent start – great people and great company. My programmer journey continued for around 5.5 years.

It was one of the most beautiful times in my life. When someone’s hobby becomes his job, it is no less than being in heaven.

During this time, I got into online technical writing and became a part of a few Mumbai technical user groups.

Early awards and achievements

I was happy with the programming, but I always knew that something is missing.

I wanted to do something bigger.

  • Shiv sir (my mentor) and I started a newspaper called “The Programmer.”
  • I actively participated as a speaker in a lot of community webinars and seminars.
  • I became a part of some open-source projects.

These contributions awarded me multiple times, including the MVP awards from CSharp corner, CodeProject, and Microsoft.

Trainer and entrepreneur

Finally, my adventurous mind made me quit my job and dragged me to the world of corporate training and consultancy. I named my company Just Compile.

Wondering why the name is “Just Compile”?

Let me be honest. It was all random, no particular theory or anything.

I did a lot of training on the various topics – Asp.net, WCF, MSBI, jQuery, HTML 5, Angular JS, Angular, ReactJS, Design pattern, Coded UI…and the list goes on.

(Did you notice Angular twice in the preceding list? Are you confused? Don’t worry. Just wait for the first chapter.)

During these days, I even finished my first book – “Learn MVC in 7 days”.

Life was much better than before. Now I was working 100% on my hobby and enjoying every bit of it.

Development company

While I was a trainer, I thought of recruiting some freshers and train them for free. My idea was if any good project gets clicked, then it will open a land of opportunities as I will be ready with the team then, or else, it would be social work. In either case, it was a win-win situation for me.

So that’s when I hired my first employee and my beloved friend Tushar Lone; Mrunali Sawant and Dipesh Shinde followed him.

Guess what; I didn’t even realize when one person company became 18 people company.

The success story of my company is firm because of my people.

They all say that I motivated them, but the truth is all of them inspired me.

Business and talent were growing in the company at a rocket speed, and I was slowly slipping away from my writing. I didn’t even realize it.

Learn Angular from Zero to 100

Then one day, while talking to Shiv sir, I realized that I moved away from my actual thing. I was a writer who used to share his experience with the world via writing. Luckily, he was always there to make me realize my mistakes.

I was dealing with the Angular framework from the very beginning as a trainer and as a programmer. I thought about starting a book on Angular, and that’s what is in your hand.

The book’s name was – Learn Angular from Zero to 100.

Is the title different?

Well, it’s a long story. I had a vision of a book. That vision eventually changed, and so did the title. That complete vision needs more than one book. Maybe very soon, you will find one or more books on Angular written by me. It will be a sequel to this book. Are you worried that this book is incomplete? Not at all. It is 100% complete. Another book that I am planning will act as a booster pack to this book.

Preface

If you are reading this book, and reading this introduction, it means that you are very serious about learning Angular. Keep up the dedication.

Two qualities (Consistency and Effort) + this book = Angular developer

This book is going to be very different from all the others that you have seen so far. I won’t say it’s better than the others. I’d say – it’s different from most.

Imagine that you are starting a train journey. You have already packed up your luggage, and you are waiting for the train to arrive at the platform. That train will take you to the world of Angular development.

Figure 0.1: Journey begins

The moment you start with Chapter 1 – Get Basics Stronger, your journey begins, and when you finish Chapter 1 – Get Basics Stronger, you will reach Station 1.

Every time you reach a new station, you will see yourself as a new person regarding Angular skills.

Your final destination will be Station 20.

Roadmap

As I’ve said before, it will be a long journey.

It has a total of 20 Stations, and by the end, when you reach Station 20, you would be strong enough to start your Angular project and call yourself an Angular developer.

Figure 0.2: Roadmap

To make it better and more organized, I have broken this journey into the following six sections:

Section 1 – This section includes one chapter and lets you travel to just one Station – Station 1. In this section, we will have a pure theory. We will touch-base on some terminologies which you hear now and then in the Angular learning world. Go through this section quickly. Maybe, a maximum of 1-1.30 hours would be enough. Don’t stress on learning everything in this chapter. Later, when you complete a couple of more chapters, things will get much easier, and then you can come back and revise. I recommend you not to skip this section and chapter.

Section 2 – In this section, we will talk about ES6 and explore some ES6 features. This section includes a total of 4 chapters and takes you to Station 2 from Station 1.

If in case you have some knowledge on ES6, then I strongly recommend you skip this section and directly start with the next section. Later, you can revisit this section, if you feel that it was a bad idea to directly jump to Section 3.

Section 3 – This section includes two chapters and takes you to Station 4 from Station 2. We will be talking about Webpack and TypeScript in this section. You can skip both the chapters if you wish. If you feel you know these concepts or believe that you know the basics and that it would be enough, don’t hesitate to skip them. (You always have an option to revisit anytime you wish.)

Section 4 – The real journey begins from this section as it includes four chapters and takes you to Station 8 from Station 4. It would be the beginning of Angular. This section will talk about creating an Angular project about including a third-party CSS library and authentication.

Section 5 – This section is one of the biggest, most complex, and most challenging sections of all. It will only take you from Station 8 to Station 10, but it includes a total of 10 chapters. This section is purely intended for Angular Services. I suggest you try the examples in this section multiple times and get used to it.

Section 6 – The last section will take you from Station 10 to Station 20 with 10 chapters. This section will cover the Angular concepts, which will finally make you an Angular developer.

A specialty of the book

Writing this book was a fantastic experience for me, and I promise that you will enjoy every bit of it. Just have patience and finish it dedicatedly.

The specialty of this book is that it’s not purely conceptual. It’s an experience.

I have been in the IT industry for more than 12 years now. I have seen a lot of technical ups and downs. I have been following Angular from the very beginning stage. I first used it when it was in the beta version.

I have trained many developers in Angular up till now and have a hands-on experience with many complex applications.

Considering all these facts, an experience that I gained in all these years deserve to be shared, and that’s what I will be doing through this book.

What will we cover in this book?

By the end of this book, you will definitely learn Angular, but the best point is that you will become an Angular developer.

Although both the statements seem the same, they are not. You know the concepts, but that doesn’t mean you can develop a project, and it doesn’t mean that you can do it with the industry’s best practices.

As I said, in this book, I will share my experience.

How to get the best benefit of this book?

(Take a snapshot of this explanation and read it multiple times during the Angular learning journey.)

As an independent consultant, I have to deal with a lot of technologies now and then. I cannot spend months or years learning any technology. It has to be quick and perfect. That made me understand what real learning is. Follow the following basic rules, and trust me, you will be a lot happier in your quest to learning Angular.

  • The first golden principle of any learning is that you cannot learn anything in one go. It takes multiple iterations. So, if needed, read certain things in this book numerous times.
  • Get into a habit of revising the previous chapters now and then.
  • Do not worry much about the theoretical concepts in the beginning. Try to understand as much as you can, and then move on to the practicals.

  • If you don’t understand something, then don’t worry much. Proceed and go through it again in the future.

    Try to recollect your school days. When you were in the 7th standard, there were some topics which you must have felt were very difficult. But a few years later, when you saw those 7th standard topics, you felt they were so easy.

    Did you ever wonder why? It’s because your brain was adjusted to it now. Your mind was accustomed to doing more advanced things; hence, the past concepts became more comfortable and easier.

    The same principle applies to every learning. You may feel some topics to be difficult at the beginning. Give yourself some time to move ahead. After a few days/months, or maybe just a few hours, plan to revisit it, and you will feel it they are much easier to understand than before. Some topics may ultimately be a bouncer to you. No issue at all. Move ahead. You will encounter a situation in the project when you realize what that topic was all about.

So, the best way to benefit from this book is – trust yourself, revise from time to time, and practice all the labs honestly and repeatedly. Read the explanations more than once.

Secondly, take the shortcuts when necessary. Your time is very important. As I said before, choose your sections wisely. Feel free to skip the second and third sections, if needed.

Journey to Angular
Development

Section 1

CHAPTER 1

Get Your Basics Stronger

Introduction

Finally, the long wait is over. The train has just arrived at the platform. Get into it. It will take you to the first Station, making your fundamentals stronger.

The plan will be as follows:

  1. To understand what this series is all about.
  2. To learn about the terminologies connected to Angular learning.
  3. To understand the role of Node.js in Angular application development.

Figure 1.1

This Station will be all theory. Don’t stress much to learn everything in this chapter in one go. You can revisit it in the future and revise it. Just relax and enjoy the learning.

Understanding what this series is all about

While going through this series, if somebody asks you, what are you learning, then don’t answer it as AngularJS because these series have nothing to do with AngularJS. It is going to be an Angular series.

Figure 1.2

AngularJS and Angular?

First of all, we have to understand whether Angular and AngularJS are the same or not.

As you know, Telephone and Mobile phone are two different things.

Figure 1.3

The telephone was introduced a long time ago to the world, and it was intended to connect people. It did the job very well.

Years passed, and a new device was launched with the same core purpose but in a much convenient way and with a lot of great features. It was the Mobile phone.

Are the Telephone and the Mobile phone the same? The answer is no.

A similar answer can be considered for Angular and Angular JS.

AngularJS is a client-side framework created by the Google team for making a single page application development.

After some time, an improved version of the same was introduced.

This new version enforced a modern UI development methodology (component-oriented architecture).

It was better in terms of performance, and the code was much organized and manageable.

It was introduced with a completely new approach. It is named Angular, and its first version was 2.0.

Is there any similarity between them?

AngularJS and Angular do share some standard vocabularies/features.

In both the technologies, you will see the Directives, Pipes, Services, and many other standard features.

Both share the collective thoughts of the Single Page Application. The concepts in both the technologies share a similar idea, but the syntax will be entirely different.

Is there a migration path from the AngularJS app to an Angular app?

Yes, there is, and it is called Re-create. 😊

Many people may argue that the AngularJS application can be migrated to the Angular application, but it’s practically a myth. It’s only possible with a trial or demo applications. With the real-time applications, it’s just a dream. They both have very different ways of programming style, syntaxes.

Terminologies connected to Angular learning

If you have ever tried to learn Angular before, you must have come across some exciting words such as Node, TypeScript, and ES6. Let’s talk about a couple of those terminologies.

Figure 1.4

Please note that if you find the initial theory a little difficult to digest, don’t worry, relax, and continue. Once you start with the practical labs, these theories will become simpler.

JavaScript

Probably many of you already know what JavaScript is. It is a programming language that has been used by developer for many years for the client-side scripting in web applications. The primary purpose of it is DOM manipulation. The JavaScript executes in the client-side by the browser, and manipulates the client DOM.

Figure 1.5

How is JavaScript different, compared to the other programming languages?

Like most programming languages, JavaScript is not a compiled language. It’s a dynamic and interpreted language. The run-time environment (provided by the browser) executes each line one by one and throws an error at run-time if anything goes wrong.

Let’s do a demo to understand the same. Create an HTML file with the following content:

  1. <html>
  2. <head></head>
  3. <body>
  4.      <script>
  5.          console.log(‘A’); console.log(‘B’);
  6.          console.log(‘C’); console.log(ABCD);
  7.          console.log(‘D’); console.log(‘E’);
  8.      </script>
  9. </body>
  10. </html>

Now, execute the HTML file. (Simply double click the file, and open it in the browser.)

As you can see, although there is an error in the fourth console.logstatement, the first three lines are executed successfully.

If it were C# or Java, we would have encountered a very different output. We would have ended up with the compile-time error. That’s JavaScript.

Figure 1.6

ES6

ES6, ES2015, and ECMA 2015 are all the same. Initially, it was proposed as ES6, and finally, ES2015 became the official name. Usually, most people call it ES6, so we will call it ES6 throughout this series.

It’s a new JavaScript standard. A lot of new capabilities and features are added in this version to make the JavaScript developer’s life easier. We will explore a couple of those features moving forward in this series.

What is and why the Single Page Application?

Gmail and Facebook are some of the most known examples of such applications. Let’s compare the traditional web applications with the Single Page Applications (SPAs).

Figure 1.7

Figure 1.8

In the case of SPA, the performance will be much better. The end-user gets one page in the beginning, and it stays forever. All the future operations performed by the end-user look like a simple DOM manipulation. Something gets dynamically visible, something gets invisible, some new items get created, and some existing items get removed, but the entire UI never gets refreshed. It gives a feeling that the whole application is developed on one single page. Hence, it’s called the Single Page Application.

Does it involve only one page?

But the question is, does it internally contain only one page? I mean, do you think that a developer developed the entire application as a single page in reality? The answer is No. It’s not possible.

In reality, for the developer, it will be a multi-page application. He/she will create multiple pages internally. After that, using the concepts like Ajax, CSS, and JavaScript, he/she brings the appearance of a Single Page application, and thus improves the overall user experience of the application. For the end-user, it will be a single-page application.

What’s the challenge for creating a SPA?

The DOM manipulation is not very easy with Vanilla JavaScript. It is a name given by the community where the code is written purely with the core JavaScript syntax (no third-party libraries).

Creating a real-time web application with a pure VanillaJavaScript will be challenging as we have to write a lot of JavaScript to achieve it altogether. Secondly, we need to focus on the browser compatibility too.

The libraries such as jQuery make the DOM manipulation very easy.

Is jQuery or some other DOM manipulation library enough for creating a SPA?

Try to imagine the volume of JavaScript we will write to create a SPA – All the DOM manipulation will be done at the client-side. The Server-Side code will only be limited to the business logic and data.

If we follow the Vanilla JavaScript or libraries such as jQuery for this purpose, the code gets challenging to manage, as there is no enforced separation of concern in the code. As the application grows bigger, the JavaScript code gets bigger and bigger, and challenging to manage.

I am not saying that we cannot create a SPA using jQuery or some other DOM manipulation library. We can but having too much JavaScript code makes the code unmanageable. We need some kind of standard and structured way of UI development.

You must have heard of the Architecture patterns such as MVC or MVVM in the server-side technologies, which provide a clear separation between the various logical areas of an application. It has a clear answer for, “What to be kept where?” and “What will talk to what.” The code is more manageable when the application is developed using such architectures.

Using jQuery, we only get a few methods that will make our life easy in terms of DOM Manipulation, but what about the code management and architecture. Don’t you think we need a better-structured approach on the client-side as well? Especially when we know that we are finally going to end up with a lot of JavaScript code.

So, the answer to the current question is, No. jQuery is not enough to build a SPA. We need more than that. We need some kind of framework that will enforce a structured way of coding in the UI world.

What is Angular?

Angular is a client-side framework created by Google. Please note, it’s not an alternative for JavaScript. It is a JavaScript framework.

Note: It’s not a library. It’s a framework.

The framework is a bigger concept than the library.

Figure 1.9

It provides a comprehensive platform needed for the development. That platform may consist of some reusable libraries to make the life easier, but it may give you many other things, such as compilers, execution environment. It may even force you to follow a certain kind of fixed structure while coding.

The Angular framework, just like jQuery, makes the DOM manipulation very easy, but it also gives you a clear separation between UI, UI logic, presentation logic, and application logic.

Angular also forces us to develop our entire UI application in terms of reusable and composable web components. It’s called the Component Oriented Architecture. It’s a standard way of UI development recommended by HTML 5.

So, in short, Angular is a client-side framework meant for creating SPA.

What is Node.js?

When I was learning Angular for the first time, I was quite confused. I wondered what Node.js is doing here, and I believe many of you share a similar confusion.

Before we dig into the question, “What is the role of Node.js in Angular application development?”, let’s first understand what Node.js is.

It’s the run-time for executing the JavaScript code. It means, now we can write the JavaScript code that can run outside the browser. With Node.js, we can create other kinds of applications, such as a desktop or even servers that can respond to the HTTP requests, and so on, using JavaScript as a language.

Installation

You can download the latest version of Node.js from the following link:

https://Node.js.org/en/download/

To confirm that the installation is successful, open the Command Prompt, and execute the following two commands one by one:

  1. node command

    You should get the following output:

  • npm is not recognized as an internal or external command.

A quick demo of the Node console application

Open your favorite text editor, and write the following code:

  1. var a=10;
  2. var b=20;
  3. console.log(a+b);

Save your file as firstnode.js.

Now, open the Command Prompt. Navigate to the folder where you have saved the file, and execute the following command:

  1. node firstnode.js

You will get the following output:

Figure 1.14

As you can see, the JavaScript code was executed without a browser.

It was a simple demonstration of a Node.jsapplication.

The Node run-time understands all the JavaScript keywords (except UI specific keywords such as alert or document), and knows how to execute it. The Node.js even understands the new ES6 features and, to some extent, ES7 (version going to be introduced after ES6).

(It was a quick demo to showcase that using Node.js, we can execute JavaScript without a browser.)

What is npm?

When we talk about the application, we have dependencies.

For instance, let’s say we are working on an application called App1, and we want to use a third-party module called dep1. That dep1 is dependent on two other third-party modules dep2 and dep3. dep3 is dependent on dep4.

Now the challenge here is, as the App1 developer, it becomes our responsibility to download dep2, dep3, and dep4 along with dep1.

In short, we need to have a complete idea about the entire dependency hierarchy. We also need to make sure that the correct version is downloaded. For instance, dep2 has the latest version as 3.5, and dep1 requires version 2.3 of dep2.

Isn’t it too much work? A simple solution is the package manager. It is a software tool that will simplify working with the dependencies. You will find the concept of the package manager mostly in all the technologies. In Java, we have Maven. In .net, we have Nuget, and in Python, we have Pep. Node has it too, and that is npm.

Using npm, we can download the various JavaScript packages from the npm registry referred to as the node modules.

The npm registry is an online database that holds the node modules.

These node modules include both the reusable libraries and the utilities. The libraries can be used in some applications, whereas, the utilities can do some automation.

npm for downloading JavaScript libraries

To demonstrate this, let’s download jquery using npm. For that, open Command Prompt, and execute the following command:

  1. npm install jquery

Now, open the folder where you executed the preceding command. You will find the node_modules folder created inside it. Inside the node_modules folder, you will discover jQuery.

As you can see, using the npm utility, we can download the reusable libraries from the npm registry. Just like jQuery, we can download Angular, ReactJS, and the other libraries easily using npm.

npm for downloading utilities

The JavaScript packages, also known as the node modules, are not limited to the third party libraries. It can be some executable applications as well.

For instance, we have a node module called webpack, which will let us bundle all our JS files and create a single bundled js file. What is bundling, and what is webpack and so on… don’t worry about these questions right now. We will talk about it soon.

For now, let’s have a demo of downloading a node module, which is an executable application.

Simply execute the following command:

  1. npm install -g @just-compile/jc_calc

You may notice an attribute -g is added to the npm install. It means, we are installing our node modules globally. (We will discuss the difference between the global and local installation later.)

(In the Windows machine, you can find the installation at C:\Users\{username}\AppData\Roaming\npm.)

As soon as the preceding command finishes its execution, we will get a new CLI command add_jc_calc. Let’s use it.

  1. add_jc_calc 8 9

You will get the following output:

  1. 17

What is package.json?

It is a simple text file that contains the metadata information about the Node.js application.

It will be situated in the root directory of the application.

We have the following three advantages of using it:

  1. To provide metadata information about our package or application.
  2. To keep track of application dependencies.
  3. For creating npm scripts.

How does package.json keep metadata information about our package or application?

Let’s start by creating package.json. It can be created manually using any text editor or the npm utility.

Open the Command Prompt, navigate to some folder, and execute the following command:

  1. npm init

It will ask for a couple of inputs.

Check the following image for reference:

Figure 1.15

In the final prompt, type yes, and press the Enter key. Open the folder in the file explorer, and you will notice the package.json created in the folder with the following content:

  1. {
  2.    “name”: “myapp”,
  3.    “version”: “1.5.1”,
  4.    “description”: “trying package.json for learning”,
  5.    “main”: “index.js”,
  6.    “scripts”: {
  7.      “test”: “echo \”Error: no test specified\” && exit 1”
  8.   },
  9.    “author”: “sukesh marla”,
  10.    “license”: “ISC”
  11. }

As you can see, package.json contains a lot of information about our application, and that’s the first advantage – keep the metadata about the application.

How is package.json used for keeping track of the application dependencies, and what’s the benefit of it?

First, let’s answer why we want to keep track of the application dependencies, and then let’s answer how.

Let’s talk about a random system dependent on three external libraries – jquery, systemjs, and core-js.

Each of these libraries can be downloaded using the following npm install commands:

  1. npm install jquery
  2. npm install systemjs
  3. npm install corejs

Now, when we say application, there will be multiple developers. Each developer needs a copy of the source code. Hence, it’s recommended to keep the entire source code in some kind of source control repository such as GitHub, bit bucket, and so on.

As the best practice, the library files won’t be included inside the source control repository; hence, every developer will be asked to download them separately using npm.

Figure 1.16

The problem with this approach is, every developer needs to download every file. In the preceding case, it’s just three libraries, but in some cases, it may be 100. In that case, there is a high possibility that he/she forgets to download some.

The solution to the preceding problem is package.json. Follow the following steps:

  1. Create package.json following the ways specified in the previous section (that is, npm init).

  2. Execute the following commands one after the other:

    a. npm install jquery --save

    b. npm install systemjs --save

    c. npm install corejs –save

Please note the additional --save flag that is added to each install command; it will create a new section in package.json called dependencies, which looks like the following:

  1. {
  2.    “name”: “myapp”,
  3.    “version”: “1.5.1”,
  4.    “description”: “trying package.json for learning”,
  5.    “main”: “index.js”,
  6.    “scripts”: {
  7.      “test”: “echo \”Error: no test specified\” && exit 1”
  8.   },
  9.    “author”: “sukesh marla”,
  10.    “license”: “ISC”,
  11.    “dependencies”: {
  12.      “corejs”: “^1.0.0”,
  13.      “jquery”: “^3.4.1”,
  14.      “systemjs”: “^6.2.5”
  15.   }
  16. }

Now, delete the node_modules folder and execute the npm install command (in the folder where the package.json file is located). You will notice that all the dependencies will be downloaded in one go.

  1. npm install

That’s it. package.json will keep the list of all the dependencies, and every developer will simply execute the command, and they will get all the libraries. In this way, we achieved both our requirements:

  1. The libraries are not kept as a part of the source control.
  2. No one will remember what all libraries are needed in the system.

Figure 1.17

How to create npm scripts and what is the purpose of it?

We have already seen a demonstration of installing the third-party node_modules using npm install.

We also saw the executable node module’s demo, but we haven’t spoken about the -g flag used with the npm install yet. Installing the node modules with the -g flag leads to the global node modules. It will be available to all the applications, whereas when used without the -g flag, it leads to the local (application-specific) node modules. They cannot be executed directly in the Command Prompt. We need npm scripts for that purpose.

Let’s do a demo.

Step 1: Create package.json using npm init.

Step 2: For the demonstration, we will use the same @just-compile/jc_calc package.

First, uninstall the global module using the following command:

  1. npm uninstall -g @just-compile/jc_calc

Please make sure not to miss the -g flag in the preceding command.

Now, install it locally as follows:

  1. npm install @just-compile/jc_calc

Step 3: Now execute the following command:

  1. add_jc_calc 8 9

You will get the following error:

  1. ‘add_jc_calc’ is not recognized as an internal or external command,
  2. operable program or batch file.

As the package is not installed globally, you won’t get the add_jc_calc CLI directly in the Command Prompt.

We need an npm script for executing the local modules.

Step 4: Open the package.json and add/modify the script section, as follows:

  1. {
  2.    “name”: “myapp”,
  3.    “version”: “1.5.1”,
  4.    “description”: “trying package.json for learning”,
  5.    “main”: “index.js”,
  6.    “scripts”: {
  7.      “add”: “add_jc_calc”
  8.   },
  9.    “author”: “sukesh marla”,
  10.    “license”: “ISC”
  11. }

Step 5: Now, in the Command Prompt, promptly execute the npm script using the following command:

  1. npm run add 8 9

You will get the following output:

  1. C:\SukeshRND\node\package>npm run add 9 9
  2.  
  3. > package@1.0.0 add C:\SukeshRND\node\package
  4. > add_jc_calc “9” “9”
  5.  
  6. 18

Executing the local node modules is not the only use case for the npm scripts. Sometimes, we may have some commands which are complex to write and are going to be used multiple times.

Instead of using those complex commands numerous times, we can create the npm scripts, pointing to the complex commands.

Webpack

Can you imagine a real-time web application with only one JavaScript file? I don’t think you can imagine that. The real-time project is always going to have a lot of JavaScript files.

Can you imagine including all of those JavaScript files manually (especially in the case of SPA)?

It would be too much overhead.

Module loader

One solution is using the module loaders. A module loader is a library that loads the JavaScript file at run-time dynamically. One example of such a module loader is systemjs.

Module loaders can simply be downloaded using npm. For instance, for downloading system js, use the following command:

  1. npm install systemjs

Figure 1.18

The problem with the module loader is performance. Loading the JavaScript files at run-time affects the performance. In one of the future articles, we will see a nice demo of the module loader. So, for now, just try to get the idea behind the Module loader.

Module bundler

A Module bundler is a node module that takes a JavaScript file as input, and then identifies all the other JavaScript files that the input file is dependent on (directly or indirectly), and finally merges all the files and generates one single JavaScript file. It joins them in such a way that the logic inside those JavaScript files won’t get affected.

That one generated bundle file will be included in the HTML file.

Figure 1.19

How come the module bundler and the module loader understand dependency?

Don’t worry about that now. We write our code following some standards when we plan to use the module bundler or module loader. For now, just believe that somehow, somewhere in every JavaScript file, we specify the dependency with the other JavaScript files.

Won’t having one single JavaScript file affect the performance?

It will improve the performance as it replaces the multiple request calls with a single one.

If the bundle size is too big, we can configure the module bundlers to create multiple feature-wise bundles.

Is Webpack a module bundler?

Yes, webpack is a module bundler, but it’s not the only bundler. We have more. Such as Browesrify.

We will see the webpack demo in one of the upcoming articles.

Does the module bundler only bundle JavaScript files?

No, it can also bundle CSS files.

What is TypeScript? And Why?

Let’s understand this by answering a couple of more sub-questions.

  • What is Typescript?

    It’s a programming language.

  • What does it do?

    Just like most of the programming languages, TypeScript is a language with a compiler. The TypeScript compiler is a node module that can be downloaded using npm. On compilation, it generates the JavaScript code.

    Figure 1.20

  • Where can I use TypeScript?

    Typescript can be used anywhere JavaScript could be used.

    Instead of writing the JavaScript, write TypeScript, compile it, and then use the generated JavaScript.

  • Why should I write code in TypeScript instead of JavaScript?

    Writing code in TypeScript instead of JavaScript will make your life easier.

    It will give us a type-safe environment for writing the code (which isn’t possible in JavaScript), plus it has certain features that make our life easier as a programmer. We will explore those features soon in this series.

  • Isn’t learning a new language kind of overhead?

    Learning the TypeScript language is very easy for any JavaScript developer. The TypeScript language inherits its syntaxes from JavaScript only.

    • The syntax for declaring the variables and functions, assigning values, and many other things in TypeScript is the same as JavaScript.
    • Everything that you can achieve in JavaScript can be delivered in TypeScript as well.

    • The equivalent of every JavaScript function is available in TypeScript. For instance, the functions such as alert, document.getElementById, console.log can also be seen in TypeScript.

      Every Js code can be straight forward copied from a JavaScript file, and pasted into a TypeScript file, and it will be considered as the TypeScript code.

  • What about the ES6 features in the case of TypeScript?

    We will cover the ES6 features very soon. If you are working with Typescript, then the good news is that Typescript has similar features.

    Figure 1.21

    In fact, TypeScript has additional (Example – Decorators, Generics). We will be exploring most of the features throughout the series.

  • Which JavaScript code is generated on the TypeScript compilation?

    It depends on the TypeScript feature we used, and the output target version we are expecting. The TypeScript compiler has a provision to specify the target of JavaScript that we are expecting as output.

    If the TypeScript feature is available in the JavaScript target version, precisely the same code will be regenerated.

    In case, the TypeScript feature is not available in the target version of JavaScript, the Typescript compiler will generate the appropriate logic.

    You will soon see all these things in action.

  • What is the role of TypeScript in Angular learning?

    As I said before, Angular is a JavaScript framework. For creating an application using Angular, we have to write a lot of JavaScript code. As we know, writing the code in the TypeScript language instead of the JavaScript language makes our life easier. The Angular applications are recommended to be created using the TypeScript language.

It was just a quick overview of TypeScript. We have a detailed article waiting purely for TypeScript.

Role of Node.js in Angular application development

Many people who start learning Angular get confused about Node.js. They get the impression that they need to know Node.js to learn Angular.

Let’s clear that confusion. You don’t need to be a Node expert if you want to learn Angular.

We won’t be writing a single line of Node.js code inside the Angular application.

So, can I create the Angular applications without having much knowledge of Node.js?

Yes, 100%.

But that doesn’t mean we don’t want Node.js at all.

  • We will install Node.js.
  • Using npm, we will download a third-party node module using which we will create an Angular application (we will talk about it in detail in the future articles).
  • We may download some additional node modules using npm as needed.
  • We may work with a couple of npm scripts to make development, building, and deployment easier.

As an Angular developer, you should know npm, package.json, npm scripts, and the concept of node modules. That will be more than enough.

Summary

So, we have reached the Station 1. Take a quick break, and relax for some time.

So far, it was more of a theoretical learning. I promise, moving forward, it’s going to be much more exciting, and much more challenging.

Let’s list out what we have learned in this chapter:

  • We explored the various terminologies that we hear every day while learning Angular:
    • Angular JS
    • Angular
    • ES5
    • ES6
    • ES2015
    • SPA
    • Node.js
    • npm
    • package.json
    • Module bundler
    • Module loader
    • Webpack
    • TypeScript
  • We learned that Angular and Angular JS are not the same. They are two different technologies, and there is no migration path.
  • We had a quick revision on JavaScript, as a programming language developer has been used for the client-side scripting in web applications for many years. The primary purpose of it is the DOM manipulation. JavaScript executes in the client-side by the browser and manipulates the client DOM.
  • We also learned that JavaScript is not a compiled language. It is an interpreted language.
  • We introduced ES6, aka ES2015, aka ECMA 2015, which is a new JavaScript standard. (By the time you are reading this book, there may be a more recent version introduced.)
  • We learned about SPA, and learned how it improves user experience. We also learned that the SPA is not an application with one page.
  • We learned that Angular is a framework by Google, meant for creating SPA in a Component-Oriented style. We learned that it is not a replacement for JavaScript; instead, it is a JavaScript framework.
  • We discussed about Node and learned that it provides an execution environment for the JavaScript applications.
    • Now we have the power to execute the JavaScript code without a browser.
    • We cleared the fact that to learn Angular in-depth, Node.js knowledge is not needed.
    • As an Angular developer, you should know npm, package.json, npm scripts, and the concept of node_modules. That will be more than enough.
  • We learned about npm, which is a Node package manager.
    • Using it, we can install the third party node modules into our application.
    • It also helps us to execute the node scripts.
  • We learned about package.json, which is a configuration file for the npm command.
    • Using it, we can define metadata information about our package or application.
    • Using it, we can keep track of application dependencies.
    • Using it, we can create npm scripts.
