Summary

So finally, after so much thinking and coding, we were successful in implementing CustomerService. Let’s list all the topics we have covered in this chapter:

  • We used the HttpClient service again in our application.
  • We used the generic version of the HttpClient.get and the post method.
  • We saw the demonstration of the Subject again.
  • We discussed the token-based authentication and implemented the same in the application.
  • We discussed the json pipe. Using this pipe, we can display the content of an object using interpolation. They were only used for troubleshooting.
  • We learned that when it comes to multiple pipes, a sequence is essential.
  • We saw the demonstration of using an anonymous object as a generic parameter. It is not recommended but may be seen in the projects.
  • We learned that we use the subscribe method to get the emitted values and use the pipe method to pipe the values through the various operators that may alter the values or even stop further emitting.
  • We discussed the map operator in RxJS. Using it, we can transform the actual HTTP response to the desired one.

CHAPTER 17

Token Interceptor

Introduction

Is there anything that can be improved in the application that we have right now?

Go through the complete code once again as a revision before moving further. If you can find room for improvement, then excellent.

The problem is adding a token. Moving further, we have to do it in almost every API call. Do we have any better way to do it?

Yes, and that is the HTTP Interceptors. Using it, we can transform every outgoing request or incoming response in between.

We will create and register an interceptor in our demo, which will transform every outgoing request by adding a token in the header.

Excited to see it in action, let’s do it.

Lab – Continued – Token interceptor

Step 75: Create TokenInterceptorService

Inside the Services folder, create a new folder Interceptors and then create a new file, http.interceptor.ts, as follows:

  1. import {HttpEvent, HttpHandler, HttpInterceptor, HttpRequest}
  2.                    from ‘@angular/common/http’;
  3. import {Injectable} from ‘@angular/core’;
  4. import {Observable} from ‘RxJS’;
  5.  
  6. @Injectable()
  7. export class TokenInterceptorService implements HttpInterceptor {
  8.  
  9.    constructor() {}
  10.    intercept(req: HttpRequest<any>, next: HttpHandler): Observable<HttpEvent<any>> {
  11.  
  12.       const token = localStorage.token;
  13.       let newHeaders = req.headers;
  14.       if (token) {
  15.         // if token is not undefined
  16.          newHeaders = newHeaders.append(‘x-access-token’, token);
  17.       }
  18.  
  19.       // HttpRequests are immutable, so it cannot be altered
  20.       // Hence we are creating a clone out of it along with adding headers
  21.       const authReq = req.clone({headers: newHeaders});
  22.       return next.handle(authReq);
  23.   }
  24. }

Discussion – Continued

Does it look like a service to you?

It should be because it is a service. In the next step, we will configure the Injectors for it.

Understand the code

It is a simple code.

We have a class implementing the HttpInterceptor interface, which forces us to define the intercept method.

Inside the intercept method, we are cloning the existing HTTP request because we cannot modify the HTTP request directly as they are immutable. Immutable means they cannot be changed.

As you can see, we have passed the custom header to the clone method. Thus, the new request object will have the authentication headers attached to it.

Which injector should be configured for TokenInterceptorService?

As I said, we need to configure the injector for TokenInterceptorService. Otherwise, the Angular DI system won’t be able to inject the TokenInterceptorService instance. The question is, which injector should we configure?

Let’s revise our learning about Angular DI.

  1. So far, we have created a couple of services and configured both the module and the element injectors.
  2. We have used an Injectable decorator for configuring the module injector, and for the element injectors, we have used a Component decorator.
  3. So far, we have only one Angular Module in action, and that is our root Module. Hence, the only module injector we have with us is the root Injector, and it creates an application-wide singleton instance.
  4. We have configured the element injector of CustomerComponent. It creates a service instance with a scope of component life span.

In the future chapters, we will create more components and more modules and talk about the injectors once again.

Based on whatever you have learned about services, what do you think, which injector should be chosen for Interceptors?

It should be the root module injector, but this time there is a twist.

We cannot use an Injectable decorator for this purpose.

Do you remember how we configured the Injector for AuthenticationService at the very beginning?

  1. providers:[{provide: AuthenticationService, useClass: AuthenticationService}

Later, we learned that the short-syntax could be used instead of the long-syntax when both provide and useClass have the same value.

  1. Providers: [AuthenticationService]

Although an injectable decorator is the recommended approach because of the tree-shaking provision, we cannot use it as it won’t allow us to explicitly specify the DI token.

Why do we need to specify the DI token explicitly for the Token interceptors?

As we have discussed before, the interceptor lets us modify the request-response in between. Creating an interceptor is like hooking into the Angular’s default execution flow. Configuring the injectors for the interceptor won’t be as simple as it is for any regular Angular service. In the case of Interceptors, we need to specify the DI token (HTTP_INTERCEPTORS) explicitly.

How to configure the root injector without using an Injectable decorator?

So finally, you will see the configuring of the module injector with the help of the NgModule decorator.

Lab – Continued

Step 76: Configure the Injector

Configure the root module injector in AppModule as follows:

  1. import {HttpClientModule, HTTP_INTERCEPTORS} from ‘@angular/common/http’;
  2. ……
  3. import {TokenInterceptorService} from ‘./Services/Interceptors/http.interceptor’;
  4. @NgModule({
  5.    ……
  6.    providers: [{provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS, useClass: TokenInterceptorService}],
  7.    bootstrap: [AppComponent],
  8. })
  9. export class AppModule {}

Step 77: Check the output

As we are done with everything, it’s time to check the output. Switch to the browser and check the output.

You get the best output so far. “A white screen.”

Figure 17.1

Check developer tools. You will find a new kind of error.

Figure 17.2

We will talk about the multi providers in the next chapter. For now, let’s finish this lab.

Step 78: Convert the regular provider to a multi-provider

For that, attach the multi attribute to the provider with the value as true.

  1. ……
  2.    providers: [{provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS,
  3.                useClass: TokenInterceptorService, multi:true}],
  4.    bootstrap: [AppComponent],
  5. })
  6. export class AppModule {}

Step 79: Cleanup CustomerService

We are not required to inject the token into the request explicitly as the token-interceptor is in place. With that, cleanup the CustomerService methods as follows:

  1. ……
  2.   private LoadCustomers(): void{
  3.      this.httpClient
  4.      .get<Array<CustomerItemResponse>>(‘http://localhost:4000/customers’).pipe(
  5.        map((customerAPIResponse) => {
  6.          return customerAPIResponse.map(
  7.            (customer) => new Customer(customer.firstName, customer.lastName));
  8.       })
  9.     ).subscribe((x) => {
  10.        this.CustomersSubject.next(x);
  11.     });
  12.   }
  13. ……
  14.    Save(customer: Customer) {
  15.      const newCustomer: NewCustomer = new NewCustomer(
  16.        customer.FName,customer.LName);
  17.      this.httpClient
  18.        .post(‘http://localhost:4000/customers’, newCustomer).subscribe(() => {
  19.          this.LoadCustomers();
  20.          this.IsAddNewSubject.next(false);
  21.       });
  22.   }
  23. ……

Step 80: Check the output

Execute and confirm that both the customer list and the data entry screen are working correctly.

Summary

Let’s list all the topics we have covered in this chapter:

  • We learned how to create and configure the HTTP interceptors.
  • We spoke about the HttpInterceptor interface, which we need to implement for creating the interceptors.
  • We learned that we could not directly modify an HTTP request in the interceptor as they are immutable. Hence, we need to clone the existing request. We attach the headers to the cloned request and then pass that cloned request further in the pipeline.
  • We saw a demonstration of both the long and the short syntax used while configuring the injectors.
  • We learned that we explicitly need to specify the DI token – HTTP_INTERCEPTORS for configuring the injectors for the HTTP interceptors.
  • We learned that, although an injectable decorator is the recommended approach because of the tree-shaking provision, we cannot use it all the time for configuring the module injectors as it won’t allow us to specify the DI token explicitly.
  • We also learned the benefit of configuring the injectors using the NgModule decorator. It provides more configuration options compared to the Injectable decorator.
  • We learned that the injector needs to be configured with multi providers for the HTTP interceptors.

CHAPTER 18

Multi Providers

Introduction

In this chapter, we will discuss multi providers. This chapter can be skipped for now if you want.

Regular providers

After looking at the previous error in Chapter 17: Token Interceptor, you must have understood that there is more than one kind of provider in Angular.

There is a regular provider, and then there is a multi-provider.

The provider we defined for CustomerService, AuthenticationService, and AuthGuard all falls under the regular providers.

It means, for one DI Token, one provider will be defined.

Multi Providers

For one DI token, multiple providers will be defined. When one DI token is expected to be injected in the application, the injector injects an array.

Let’s do a quick RND to understand the same.

Create a new service MultiRndService as follows:

  1. @Injectable()
  2. export class MultiRndService{
  3.      m1(){
  4.        console.log(‘MultiService1’);
  5.     }
  6. }

Now, create one more service, MultiRndService2, as follows:

  1. @Injectable()
  2. export class MultiRndService2{
  3.      m2(){
  4.        console.log(‘MultiService2’);
  5.     }
  6. }

Now, configure the root Injector with a regular provider as follows:

  1. …….
  2.    providers: [{provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS,
  3.             useClass: TokenInterceptorService, multi: true},
  4.      {provide:MultiRndService, useClass: MultiRndService},
  5.      {provide:MultiRndService, useClass: MultiRndService2},
  6.   ],
  7.    bootstrap: [AppComponent],
  8. })
  9. export class AppModule {}

As you can see, we have used the same DI token for both the providers.

Next, specify a parameter of the type MultiRndService in the constructor of Customer Component.

  1. ……
  2. constructor(private customerService: CustomerService,
  3.                private authenticationService: AuthenticationService,
  4.                private rndService: MultiRndService
  5.               ) {
  6.      const decodedToken = jwt_decode(localStorage.token);
  7. ……

Now, put a breakpoint inside the constructor, and let’s check what gets injected.

Figure 18.1

You can see that the instance of the MultiRndService2 class got injected.

Before we proceed, I want to make your life easier by explaining how an incompatible type (MultiRndService2) was injected.

Well, remember the injection happens at runtime, and at runtime, everything is JavaScript, so no matter what you expect, anything can be injected.

Hence, the value in the provide and useClass doesn’t need to be compatible with each other.

In a real-time system, I would have defined a base class or an interface on top of both the types and used it as a DI token.

Now, let’s get back to our research. Attach the multi attribute with the true value to both the providers and check the output.

  1. providers: [{provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS,
  2.   useClass: TokenInterceptorService, multi: true}
  3.      ,{provide:MultiRndService, useClass: MultiRndService, multi: true},
  4.      {provide:MultiRndService, useClass: MultiRndService2, multi: true},
  5.   ],

Figure 18.2

As you can see, this time, the instances of both the classes got injected in the form of an array.

What happens if we specify one of them as a multi-provider and one as a regular?

We will get a “cannot mix multi providers and regular providers” error in such a case.

Why are we getting the “cannot mix…” error while configuring the Injector for HTTP_INTERCEPTOR?

We created an HTTP interceptor in Chapter 17: Token Interceptor and then configured the module injector. The important point is we did it only once.

We have not created the multiple providers for HTTP_INTERCEPTOR.

If that is the case, why did we get the “cannot mix…” error when we created a regular provider?

If you remember, in one of the previous labs, we imported HttpClientModule in our AppModule.

(Check the imports section of the NgModule decorator in AppModule.)

When we import one Angular module into another, providers get merged. So in our case, all the providers defined in the HttpClientModule got merged to the providers of AppModule.

Angular has already configured the injector for the DI token HTTP_INTERCEPTOR with a multi-provider in the NgModule decorator of HttpClientModule.

That’s why we got a “cannot mix…” error when we configured the injector with the regular provider.

Don’t you think rndService parameter of constructor should be declared as an Array?

The question is, aren’t we supposed to write the CustomerComponent constructor as follows:

  1. ……
  2.    constructor(private customerService: CustomerService,
  3.                private authenticationService: AuthenticationService,
  4.                private rndService: Array<MultiRndService>
  5.               ) {
  6. ……

If we pursue it, we will get the following error:

Figure 18.3

We need to define a provider for Array. Though it seems logical for any strongly typed language developer, it will make our life more complicated.

In such cases, we use the Injection Token or the String Token instead of the Type Token.

DI Tokens

Do you remember our discussion of the DI token?

We learned that the injector uses a token to identify the correct provider when injecting in the application.

We also specified three kinds of tokens – Type Token, String Token, and Injection Token.

So far, we were using the type token.

But there are scenarios where we won’t be able to specify the type as a token. Such as the one mentioned earlier.

So in such cases, we use the String token or the Injection token.

String token example

Configure the injector with a provider but instead of the type token, use the string token.

  1. ……
  2.    providers: [{provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS,
  3. useClass: TokenInterceptorService, multi: true}
  4.      , {provide: “RND_VALUE”, useClass: MultiRndService, multi: true},
  5.      {provide: “RND_VALUE”, useClass: MultiRndService2, multi: true},
  6.   ],
  7.    bootstrap: [AppComponent],
  8. })
  9. export class AppModule {}

Next, change the component’s constructor as follows:

  1. constructor(private customerService: CustomerService,
  2.                private authenticationService: AuthenticationService,
  3.                @Inject(“RND_VALUE”)x: Array<MultiRndService>
  4.               ) {

You will notice a specialized decorator is attached to the constructor parameter now – Inject.

@Inject() is a manual mechanism for letting Angular know that a parameter must be injected.

The best thing is the parameter type. It is an Array of MultiRndService.

Debug like earlier, and you will notice both the Service instances are injected as an Array.

Injection token example

Using the magic strings is always considered a bad practice in programming. Using a String token is also regarded as a bad practice, as there is a chance of spelling mistakes and therefore, run time errors.

So the recommended approach is using the Injection token instead.

To do that, first of all, declare a const variable of the type InjectionToken as follows. (It’s just RND, so define it in the same file where you have created MultiRNDService.)

  1. export const RND_TOKEN = new InjectionToken<MultiRndService[]>
  2. (‘CollectionOfRNDService’);

Next, change the provider as follows:

  1. ……
  2. import {MultiRndService, MultiRndService2, RND_TOKEN} from ‘./Services/multi-rnd.service’;
  3. @NgModule({
  4.    ……
  5.    providers: [{provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS,
  6.        useClass: TokenInterceptorService, multi: true}
  7.      // ,{provide: “RND_VALUE”, useClass: MultiRndService, multi: true},
  8.      // {provide: “RND_VALUE”, useClass: MultiRndService2, multi: true},
  9.      ,{provide: RND_TOKEN, useClass: MultiRndService, multi: true},
  10.      {provide: RND_TOKEN, useClass: MultiRndService2, multi: true},
  11.   ],
  12.    bootstrap: [AppComponent],
  13. })
  14. export class AppModule {}

There is no more hard coded string anywhere. If there is any spelling mistake, we will get a compile error.

Finally, change the component constructor as follows:

  1. constructor(private customerService: CustomerService,
  2.                private authenticationService: AuthenticationService,
  3.               // @Inject(“RND_VALUE”)x: Array<MultiRndService>
  4.                @Inject(RND_TOKEN)x: Array<MultiRndService>
  5.               ) {

Do the same debugging to check the output.

Why do we need a multi-provider?

Now you know what a multi-provider is.

You know how to create a multi-provider.

The final question is why do we need it?

We need it sometimes when we are creating reusable services.

Now, let’s say that a part of the service logic will be defined as a part of the library itself, and a part of it will be provided by the one who uses the library. Using the multi-providers becomes essential.

Summary

Let’s review the topics that we have learned in this chapter:

  • We learned that it is possible to define more than one provider for a single DI token. This is referred to as a multi-provider.
  • We learned that if the multiple regular providers are defined for a single DI token, one provider will replace the other based on the order.
  • We learned that if multiple multi-providers are defined for a single DI token, the injector will inject an array of services.
  • We learned that while defining a provider, the DI token and the actual services are not expected to be compatible. They can have a completely different structure.
  • We learned that we could not define both the regular provider and the multi-provider for a single DI token. Either all the providers should be regular, or all should be multi for a single DI token.
  • We learned that using the String or Injection token with multi-providers is recommended as DI token instead of Type token.
  • We learned about the Inject decorator that lets us manually tell Angular that the parameter has to be injected. It will be used in the case of String and Injection token.
  • We learned that a multi-provider could be very useful sometimes if we are creating a reusable service.

CHAPTER 19

Compile-time Configuration

Introduction

If you have any application development experience, you must have already figured out the drawback of the current application. The API URL is embedded directly inside the app, which will trouble us a lot in the long run.

We may have different API URLs in the production mode. The current code will be too difficult as we have to change it in every place. We need some configuration mechanisms in the project, and that’s what we will be learning to do in this chapter.

Compile-time versus run-time configuration

Compile-time configuration means that the configuration will be done at the time of compilation, and the run-time configuration means it will be done at the time of deployment.

If you’re confused, don’t worry. Let’s do the demo and understand both.

Lab – Continued – Compile time configuration

Step 81: Create the second server

The first step will be creating another server to confirm that the configuration changes are working.

For that, quickly create a new JavaScript file in the server folder and call it newServer.js.

Copy everything from the existing server.js and put it into the newServer.js.

Don’t worry about the code inside it. Just change the port and the default customer collection to some other value.

  1. ……
  2. const port = process.env.PORT || 5000;
  3. ……
  4. let customers = [
  5.    {customerId: 1, firstName: “A”, lastName: “B”},
  6.    {customerId: 2, firstName: “C”, lastName: “D”},
  7.    {customerId: 3, firstName: “E”, lastName: “F”},
  8. ];

Step 82: Run server

Now open a new Command Prompt, navigate to the server folder, and run this new server by executing the following command:

  1. node newServer.js

Now, we have two servers running—one with port 4000 and the second with 5000; both of which are returning a different set of values.

Discussion – Continued

Angular has a provision for compile-time configuration. Inside the src folder, there is a folder called environments. It contains two files, environment.ts, and environment.prod.ts, with the following content:

  1. // environment.ts
  2. export const environment = {
  3.    production: false
  4. };
  1. // environment.ts
  2. export const environment = {
  3.    production: true
  4. };

As you can see, it exports a constant object called the environment with a single property – production.

Lab – Continued

Step 83: Create an apiURL key in the environment

Create a new key apiURL in both the environment.ts and the environment.prod.ts files, as follows:

  1. // environment.ts
  2. export const environment = {
  3.    production: false,
  4.    apiUrl: ‘http://localhost:4000’,
  5. };
  1. // environment.prod.ts
  2. export const environment = {
  3.    production: true,
  4.    apiUrl: ‘http://localhost:5000’,
  5. };

As you can see, we are pointing to the old server in one file and the new one in another.

Step 84: Get Api Url dynamically in service

Change the LoadCustomers method in CustomerService as follows:

  1. private LoadCustomers(): void{
  2.      this.httpClient
  3.      .get<Array<CustomerItemResponse>>(`${environment.apiUrl}/customers`)
  4.      .pipe(
  5.        map((customerAPIResponse) => {
  6.          return customerAPIResponse.map(
  7.            (customer) => new Customer(customer.firstName, customer.lastName)
  8.         );
  9.       })
  10.     ).subscribe((x) => {
  11.        this.CustomersSubject.next(x);
  12.     });
  13.   }
  14. ……

As you can see, instead of a fixed API URL, now we have a dynamic URL coming from the configuration.

Step 88: Rebuild the application in production mode

Stop lite-server, navigate the root folder of the application, and rebuild the app again. But this time, use the --prod flag. It will create an optimized production-ready application build.

Figure 19.3

This time dist\lab4-ng folder will contain fewer items than before.

Discussion – Continued

  • One difference between the production build and the non-production build is, in the production build, the source map files (files with extension map.js) are missing. The source-map files contain the information about the source TypeScript files. The source map files are the reason why we are able to debug the TypeScript files directly in the browser.

  • The second difference is, the vendor.js file is not generated in the production-build. This file was meant to contain the third-party libraries imported into the app.

    The main bundle is optimized during the production-build. All the unused code is removed from it while generating the final bundle; hence, for the production-build, the vendor build is integrated into the main bundle.

Step 89 – Check the application

Once again, start lite-server and check the output. This time, you will see the customer records coming from the server running on port 5000 port.

This proves that instead of environment.ts, environment.prod.ts got considered.

It is referred to as a compile-time configuration. At the compile-time, the application is configured with an API URL. (Also modify the Save function and do the test.)

Summary

Let’s review the topics that we have learned in this chapter:

  • We began our chapter by understanding the need for configuration in the application.
  • We learned the difference between the compile-time and the run-time configuration. The compile-time configuration means that the configuration will be done at the time of compilation, and the run-time configuration means it will be done at the time of deployment.
  • We learned about the environment.ts file and how it gets replaced with the environment.prod.ts file in the production mode.
  • We generated the non-production mode and production mode builds of our Angular application using the ng build and ng build --prod command, respectively.
  • We learned that in the non-production build, Angular CLI also generates the source map files; thus, we can directly debug the TypeScript files at run-time.
  • We learned that we wouldn’t get a separate vendor.js file in the production build as it is integrated into the main bundle.
  • We saw a demonstration of an Angular module called lite-module that can be used as a development purpose web-server for our static files.

CHAPTER 20

Run-time Configuration

Introduction

In the previous chapter, we spoke about the compile-time configuration.

But in some situations, the run-time configures suits better. In this chapter, we will learn how to do it.

Lab – Continued – Run-time configuration

Step 90: Create a configuration file

Create a new file config.json in the src/assets folder with the following content:

  1. {
  2.    “apiUrl”: “http://localhost:4000”
  3. }

Discussion

Why the assets folder?

You must be wondering why we explicitly put our file inside the assets folder.

As you know, in the current lab, we are planning to bring the run-time configuration into action.

For that, we need the config.json file as it is in the final build.

A fantastic thing about the ng build command is that the assets folder will be replicated into the final build as it is.

Are you wondering why the assets folder is so special?

You will find the answer to that question in the angular.json file.

Figure 20.1

Did you notice the assets section inside the build section?

Inside it, we have specified our assets folder as one of the values. All the folders and the files defined inside this section will be copied into the final build by Angular CLI as it is.

Lab – Continued

Step 91: Create AppConfigService

Next, create a file with the name app-config.service.ts file in the Services folder as follows:

  1. import {HttpClient} from ‘@angular/common/http’;
  2. import {Injectable} from ‘@angular/core’;
  3. import {Subscription} from ‘RxJS’;
  4. @Injectable({
  5.    providedIn: ‘root’
  6. })
  7. export class AppConfigService {
  8.    apiUrl: string;
  9.    constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}
  10.    loadConfig(): Subscription {
  11.      return this.http
  12.        .get<{apiUrl: string}>(‘./assets/config.json’)
  13.        .subscribe(config => {
  14.          this.apiUrl = config.apiUrl;
  15.       });
  16.   }
  17. }

Step 92: Get API URL dynamically in service

Inject AppConfigService into the CustomerService as follows:

  1. ……
  2. export class CustomerService {
  3. ……
  4.    constructor(private appConfigService: AppConfigService,
  5.                private httpClient: HttpClient) {
  6. ……
  7.   }
  8. ……

Step 93: Make API call with dynamic URL

Next, change the LoadCustomers method as follows:

  1. ……
  2.    private LoadCustomers(): void{
  3.      this.httpClient
  4.      .get<Array<CustomerItemResponse>>(`${this.appConfigService.apiUrl}
  5. /customers`)
  6.      .pipe(
  7.        map((customerAPIResponse) => {
  8.          return customerAPIResponse.map(
  9.            (customer) => new Customer(customer.firstName, customer.lastName)
  10.         );
  11.       })
  12.     )
  13.      .subscribe((x) => {
  14.        this.CustomersSubject.next(x);
  15.     });
  16.   }
  17. ……

As you can see, now, the API URL is not hardcoded anymore.

Step 94: Check the output

Check the output in the browser. Do you get an empty table? Of course, you did. 😊

Check the developer tool. You will see the following error:

Figure 20.2

Discussion – Continued

Why did we get this error?

As you know, the LoadConfig method of AppConfigService is what sets the value to the apiURL property. Surprisingly, we have not invoked that method anywhere so far. Hence, apiURL is undefined.

Do you know what exactly we want?

We want the apiUrl property to be updated with a value in the config.json file before any external API calls are made.

How can we do that?

We have to invoke the LoadConfig method before the Angular marks the application as initialized. That way, we get 100% assurance that the apiURL property will be updated before any component is loaded.

In short, we need a provision to hook into the Angular’s initialization process and write our custom code.

Is this possible?

In Angular, we have a provision for hooking into the Angular’s bootstrap process.

We can configure a function that gets injected into an application startup and executed during the application initialization. In case that function returns a promise, the initialization does not complete until the promise is resolved.

How to hook the custom logic into the Angular’s initialization process?

Did you notice the word injected in the preceding explanation? Go through it again, if you didn’t notice.

Angular has exposed a DI token of type InjectionToken called APP_INITIALIZER.

We provide our function to this token, and it automatically gets hooked into the Angular Initialization process.

How to inject function into the DI token?

We have already seen an example of creating the providers using useClass. It is when we want to provide type as the value. The Angular injector creates an instance of that type and injects it.

But there is more than useClass:

  • useFactory – This lets us provide a method as a value. It is used when we want to control the object creation manually.

    The Angular injector invokes the factory method every time it wants to do the injection. The factory method is always expected to return an object. Whatever the factory method returns, that will be injected into the application.

  • useValue – This lets us inject a static value. A value can be any scalar value or an object. It’s best to inject constant values.
  • useExisting – It is the alias provider. It is used when we want to use the new provider in place of the old provider.

In our current case, the useFactory fits well. Let’s see it in action.

Lab – Continued

Step 95: Create initializeConfig method

Create a new file app-initializer.ts in the Services folder and create a function called initializeConfig inside it as follows:

  1. export function initializeConfig() {
  2.    return () => {
  3.      return new Promise((resolve) => {
  4.        setTimeout(() => {
  5.          console.log(‘Testing’);
  6.          resolve();
  7.       }, 3000);
  8.     });
  9.   };
  10. }

Please take some time and analyze the code.

It’s a simple function that is returning another function, and that another function is returning a promise, and finally, the promise gets resolved after 3 seconds.

Step 96: Configure injector to inject initializer function

In the AppModule, configure the root injector as follows:

  1. import {HttpClientModule, HTTP_INTERCEPTORS} from ‘@angular/common/http’;
  2. import {APP_INITIALIZER, NgModule} from ‘@angular/core’;
  3. ……
  4. import {initializeConfig} from ‘./Services/app-initializer’;
  5. ……
  6. @NgModule({
  7.    declarations: [AppComponent, CustomerComponent, LoginComponent],
  8.    imports: [……],
  9.    providers: [
  10.      {provide: APP_INITIALIZER, useFactory: initializeConfig,multi:true},
  11.      {provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS, useClass: TokenInterceptorService, multi:true}
  12. ……

Step 97: Check the output

Execute the application, and you will notice a 3-second pause before CustomerComponent or LoginComponent gets displayed. If you have not clearly understood yet, then increase the period from 3 seconds to a higher number. You will find that only after the promise is resolved, the application will be considered initialized, and only after that, the component is rendered.

Step 98: Return promise from AppConfigService

The loadConfig method in AppConfigService is returning the subscription object as the subscribe method of the observable returns the subscription object. Let’s modify it to return the promise object.

  1.   loadConfig(): Promise<void> {
  2.      return this.http
  3.        .get<{apiUrl: string}>(‘./assets/config.json’).toPromise()
  4.        .then(config => {
  5.          this.apiUrl = config.apiUrl;
  6.       });
  7.   }

Step 99: Inject AppConfigService to initializeConfig method

Inject AppConfigService into InitalizeConfig by adding it as a parameter to the method. Then, invoke the loadConfig method inside it as follows:

  1. import {AppConfigService} from ‘./app-config.service’;
  2. export function initializeConfig(appConfigService: AppConfigService) {
  3.    return () => {
  4.      return appConfigService.loadConfig();
  5.   };
  6. }

Step 100: Check the output

Once again, we will get a “white screen of death.”

In the developer tools, we will find the following error:

Figure 20.3

Discussion – Continued

What exactly happened in the preceding case?

Angular, as expected, invoked the factory function during the initialization process, which is initializeConfig.

The problem is the parameter of the initializeConfig function.

In the preceding case, when the DI system invoked the factory method in Angular, no parameter was passed, and hence appConfigService is undefined, leading to the preceding error.

What to do?

We have to tell Angular somehow that our factory function is dependent on AppConfigService so that before invoking the factory function, it creates the instance of AppConfigService class and passes it, then passes it as a parameter while invoking. In short, we have to tell Angular to inject the instance of the AppConfigService class into the factory function.

That can be done using deps.

Lab – Continued

Step 101: Define the dependency

In the AppModule, while defining the factory function for APP_INITIALIZER, set the deps property to indicate that our factory function is dependent on AppConfigService.

  1. ……
  2.    providers: [
  3.      {provide: APP_INITIALIZER, useFactory: initializeConfig, multi: true, deps:[AppConfigService]},
  4. ……
  5.   ],
  6.    bootstrap: [AppComponent],
  7. ……

Step 102: Check the output

Finally, we will get the table displaying the dynamically returned customers from the server.

Discussion – Continued

Now I know, despite getting the proper output, you are not feeling comfortable.

You must be wondering why we have to explicitly specify the dependency using the deps property when it comes to useFactory. It was automatic with the useClass.

The answer is, in the case of useClass, if you remember, I said, “every consumer of the service must be decorated with the Injectable decorator.” That Injectable decorator does that automation for us. It adds the metadata to the Service class specifying other services that it depends on.

In the case of useFactory, we don’t add any such decorator. Hence, we have to do it manually, and for that, we have deps.

Lab – Continued

With the preceding step, it is confirmed that AppConfigService is working as per the expectation for LoadCustomers. Next, let’s implement the Save method in CustomerService and the authenticate method in AuthenticateService as well.

  3.      // Change no 3 - Observable is subscribed
  4.      this.httpClient
  5.        .post<AuthenticationResponse>(
  6.          `${this.appConfigService.apiUrl}/signin`,user).subscribe(……
  7. ……
  8. ……//CustomerService
  9. Save(customer: Customer) {
  10.      const newCustomer: NewCustomer = new NewCustomer(
  11.        customer.FName,
  12.        customer.LName
  13.     );
  14.      this.httpClient
  15.        .post(`${this.appConfigService.apiUrl}/customers`, newCustomer)
  16.        .subscribe(……
  17. ……

Execute, test, and confirm that both the save and the login functionality are working fine.

Summary

With this lab, we finally reached Station 9. I hope that you have now gotten a clearer picture of the run-time configuration and how it can be achieved in Angular.

It was the longest journey of all. Take a good break and give yourself a relaxing sleep. See you in the next chapter, where we will begin our journey to the next station.

In this chapter, we covered the following topics:

  • We learned that the assets folder located in the SRC folder of the Angular application would be copied to the final build.
  • We learned that we could hook into the Angular’s initialization process by configuring the root injector with a DI token provider – APP_ INITIALIZER.
  • We learned that we could provide a method as a value to the DI token using useFactory.
  • We spoke about the toPromise method of the observable class that creates a promise out of the observable.
  • We learned that while creating the providers, using the deps property, we can specify the current provider’s dependency. It is a must to explicitly define the dependency with useFactory.
  • We learned that in the case of useClass, we are not required to explicitly specify the dependent services, as an Injectable decorator does that for us. That is why, we have to attach an Injectable decorator to every service class, no matter what injector is configured for it.

CHAPTER 21

Error Handling

Introduction

In this chapter, we will begin our journey to Station 10, and by the end of this station, you will learn everything about the run-time error handling in Angular.

Before we dive into the lab, let’s understand the different kinds of run-time exceptions that an Angular application can have:

  1. Client-side errors: These are unhandled run-time errors in the client-side logic.
  2. Server-side errors: It can further be categorized into the following three areas:
    • Unhandled run-time error
    • Non-authorized error from the server
    • Server not connected error – when an HTTP call is attempted, and the server is not available

In this chapter, we will learn to handle all the four kinds of errors.

Lab – Error handling in Angular

Step 1: Rename the application

Start renaming the application from lab4-NG to lab5-NG.

Next, download the lab5 server from GitHub and execute it using the node server.js command.

This new server exposes a new endpoint for testing the server-side errors.

If we are going to handle the error, then first we need the error. So, let’s create a folder ErrorTest inside the app folder and then create a new component ErrorTesComponent inside it as follows:

  6. })
  7. export class ErrorTestComponent {
  8. }

  3. <input type=”button” value=”Server side error” (click)=”throwServerError()”>
  4. <input type=”button” value=”UnAuhthorizedError”
  5. (click)=”throwUnAuthorizedError()”>

As you can see, we have three buttons – each button leads to one kind of error discussed initially.

  1. throwClientError() {

  3. }

  1.    constructor(private appConfigService: AppConfigService,

  3.   }

Discussion – Continued

So, we have our component ready, which will throw an error and help test the error handling logic.

Next, let’s decide what we want to do when an unexpected error is encountered in the system:

  • For unexpected run-time errors (both the client and the server), the most followed involves the following two steps:
    1. Redirect the user to some custom-designed page.
    2. Persist (log) error in some storage medium, so that later it can be examined for troubleshooting.
  • For unauthorized errors, the preferred approach is, redirecting to the login screen.
  • For the failure generated because of the server’s unavailability, the preferred approach is displaying some custom messages.

So, now we know what has to be done for each kind of error.

Discussion – Continued

Now that all the ingredients are set for action, it’s time to learn how to handle the errors.

Fortunately, Angular has a centralized exception handling already set in place. The default implementation prints the error messages to the console.

The default behavior can be overridden by using a custom Angular service and injecting it into the Angular pipeline as a new error handler. Let’s do the same.

Lab – Continued

Step 15: Create the custom Error Handler

Create a new file app-error-handler.service.ts inside the Services folder with the following content:

  1. import {HttpErrorResponse, HttpResponseBase} from ‘@angular/common/http’;
  2. import {ErrorHandler, Injectable, NgZone} from ‘@angular/core’;
  3. import {Router} from ‘@angular/router’;
  4.  
  5. @Injectable()
  6. export class AppErrorsHandler implements ErrorHandler {
  7.    constructor(
  8.      private router: Router,
  9.      private zone:NgZone
  10.   ) {}
  11.  
  12.    handleError(error: Error | HttpErrorResponse) {
  13.      if (error instanceof HttpResponseBase) {
  14.        this.HandleServerSideError(error); // Indicates its a server side error
  15.     } else {
  16.        this.HandleClientSideError(error); // Indicates its a client side error
  17.     }
  18.   }
  19.  
  20.    private HandleServerSideError(error: HttpErrorResponse) {
  21.      if (error.status === 0) {
  22.        alert(‘Server is not running’);
  23.     } else if (error.status === 401) {
  24.        this.zone.run(() => this.router.navigate([‘/login’]));
  25.     } else {
  26.        localStorage.error = error.message;
  27.        this.zone.run(() => this.router.navigate([‘/error’]));
  28.     }
  29.   }
  30.    private HandleClientSideError(error: Error) {
  31.      localStorage.error = error.message;
  32.      this.zone.run(() => this.router.navigate([‘/error’]));
  33.   }
  34. }

Discussion – Continued

Let’s understand the preceding code.

The first thing you must have noticed is the ErrorHandler interface. To create a custom error handler, we must implement our class with the ErrorHandler interface and define the handleError method.

handleError method is self-explanatory. You can see the if…else condition. Out of the four errors discussed, three are handled in the if block, whereas the remaining one was handled in the else block.

Note: In our current case, we are only storing the latest error in our local storage. In the real-time scenario, you may follow a more persistent medium, such as a Database, and keep all the errors.

zone

I am sure, zone.run in the preceding code must have caught your eyes.

We have an encapsulated router.navigate inside the zone.run call.

To understand the same, look into the following code:

Figure 21.7

The preceding code is a part of the original Angular source code. onHandleError gets executed when the Angular application throws an unhandled exception.

Angular, in response to the error, makes a call to the zone.runOutsideAngular method.

zone.runOutsideAngular

In Angular, the zone provides the execution context for the application.

zone.runOutsideAngular makes the code execute outside the Angular’s execution context so that the change detection won’t kick-off. If you recall, we spoke about the change detection once earlier. We said it is responsible for updating the UI, and no change detection means no UI update.

Sometimes, to control the Angular application’s performance, we purposely execute some code outside the Angular’s execution context. That can be done using the runOutsideAngular method.

By default, Angular is only interested in displaying the exception detail in the console and not in the UI update. Hence, in the centralized error handler, it executes the code using the runOutsideAngular method.

zone.run

When you are outside of the Angular’s execution context, you can re-enter the execution zone using the zone.run method.

The preceding code depicts that the error handler executes outside the Angular context. Hence, we have used the zone.run method so that our router.navigate method performs in the original execution context of our application, and therefore we see the updated UI.

Don’t stress much to understand the preceding theory as we hardly use runOutsideAngular in real-time.

My advice is, don’t forcefully use the runOutsideAngular method in your project.

When needed, you will realize it, and secondly, once you use it, you may need to use the run method to come back to the original world.

Lab – Continued

Step 16: Configure Injector

The preceding step will be configuring the root injector with our custom error handler. Open the app.module.ts file, and modify the code to the following:

  1. import {HttpClientModule, HTTP_INTERCEPTORS} from ‘@angular/common/http’;
  2. import {APP_INITIALIZER, ErrorHandler, NgModule} from ‘@angular/core’;
  3. import {FormsModule, ReactiveFormsModule} from ‘@angular/forms’;
  4. import {BrowserModule} from ‘@angular/platform-browser’;
  5. import {RouterModule} from ‘@angular/router’;
  6. ……
  7. import {AppErrorsHandler} from ‘./Services/app-error-handler.service’;
  8. ……
  9. @NgModule({
  10. ……
  11.    providers: [
  12.      {provide: APP_INITIALIZER, useFactory: initializeConfig, multi: true, deps:[AppConfigService]},
  13.      {provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS, useClass: TokenInterceptorService, multi: true},
  14.      {provide:ErrorHandler, useClass:AppErrorsHandler},
  15. ……
  16. })
  17. export class AppModule {}

Discussion – Continued

In the preceding code, you can see that we have configured the root injector using the NgModule decorator instead of the Injectable decorator. An Injectable decorator cannot be used in this case as it won’t allow us to explicitly specify the DI token. For replacing the error handler with a custom error handler, we need to provide a DI token (ErrorHandler) explicitly.

Summary

So, we have now reached station 10. In this journey, we covered the following topics:

  • We learned that we could attach a component-specific style to a component. For that, we will use the styleUrls parameter of the Component decorator.
  • We learned that Angular has a centralized exception handling already set in place. The default implementation prints the error messages to the console.
  • We learned that the default behavior could be overridden using a custom Angular service and injecting it into the Angular pipeline as a new error handler. For that, we have to configure the root injector for the DI token – ErrorHandler.
  • We learned that we have to implement the service with the ErrorHandler interface for creating a custom error handler service.
  • We learned about zone.runOutsideAngular method that lets us execute code outside the Angular’s execution context.
  • We learned about the zone.run method that lets us get back to the Angular’s execution context.

Section 5

Summary

In Section 5, we explored the Angular services in detail and covered two stations – Station 9 and Station 10 – which completes our journey half way. Let’s revise each chapter in this section.

Chapter 12 – Authentication Service

  • We revised the DI concept again and learned that it makes our code loosely coupled, leading to more maintainable and testable code.
  • We spoke about the Angular Injector, which is responsible for injecting the service instances into the Angular application.
  • We discussed the two kinds of Injectors – Module and Element.
  • We learned that both the Injectors maintain a hierarchy.
  • We learned how to configure the service using an Injectable decorator and a Component decorator.
  • We learned that both the NgModule and the Injectable decorator let us configure the module injectors, whereas the Component decorator configures the element injector.
  • We learned that we have to add the Injectable decorator to every Angular service dependent on some other service regardless of what injector is configured.
  • We learned that the root Injector creates a global singleton instance, whereas the element injector creates the instances that will be specific to the component instance (and its children).
  • We spoke about the short syntax for configuring the injector when both the provide and the useClass have the same value.
  • We learned about the reactive programming and implementing it in Angular with the help of RxJS.
  • We learned that in reactive programming, the Observable is subscribed by a Subscriber, and the Observer feeds the data into the Observables.
  • We have seen a demonstration of the RxJS Subjects, which represents both the Observable and the Observer in the reactive programming.
  • We learned that the RxJS subjects would be marked as private in the real-time project, and the underlying observable will be exposed as a public member.

Chapter 13 – Unsubscribe

  • We learned that unsubscribing is very important as it will lead to a memory leak otherwise.
  • We learned how to unsubscribe from the RxJS subscriptions.
  • We learned about the ngOnDestroy life cycle event of the Angular component
  • We had a quick talk on the Angular pipe. It is used to encapsulate the transformation logic in Angular (a separate chapter is dedicated to it).
  • Finally, we discussed the async pipe.

Chapter 14 – Logout and Route Guard Cleanup

  • We learned about the importance of writing logic in the services by moving the existing code into the services.
  • We again revised the element and the module injector in this chapter. As the element injector was not serving our requirement, we switched it to the module injector.
  • We learned that the element injector of AppComponent would indirectly create a singleton global instance, as it will never get destroyed because it is a root component. Secondly, by being a root, the service instances created by it will be accessible to all the child components.
  • We learned that for configuring the root injector, an Injectable decorator is preferred more than the NgModule decorator as an Injectable decorator leads to tree shaking. Tree shaking is a step in the Angular build process that ensures all the unused services are removed from the final bundle.
  • We learned that we could leverage the HTML power in Angular by using the HTML’s autofocus attribute, form tag, and submit button.

Chapter 15 – Customer Service

  • We learned how to create the custom observables using the RxJS of operator
  • We saw a demonstration of configuring the element injector once again.
  • We had a revision of the RxJS Subject in Angular.
  • We learned about the RxJS Behavior Subject in Angular.
  • We learned a new way of troubleshooting/debugging the Angular apps in the developer tools using the ng object exposed by Angular.
  • We saw async as in action.
  • We saw *ngIf with else in action.
  • We discussed the challenge we face in emitting the reference types from the service.

Chapter 16 - HTTP Service

  • We used the HttpClient service again in our application.
  • We used the generic version of the HttpClient.get and the post method.
  • We saw the demonstration of the Subject again.
  • We discussed the token-based authentication and implemented the same in the application.
  • We discussed the json pipe. Using this pipe, we can display the contents of an object using the interpolation. They were only used for troubleshooting.
  • We learned that when it comes to multiple pipes, a sequence is essential.
  • We saw the demonstration of using an anonymous object as a generic parameter. It is not recommended but may be seen in the projects.
  • We learned that we use the subscribe method to get the emitted values and use the pipe method to pipe the values through the various operators that may alter the values or even stop further emitting.
  • We discussed the map operator in RxJS. Using it, we can transform the actual HTTP response to the desired one.

Chapter 17 - Token Interceptor

  • In this chapter, we learned how to create and configure the HTTP interceptors.
  • We spoke about the HttpInterceptor interface, which we need to implement for creating the interceptors.
  • We learned that we could not directly modify an HTTP request in the interceptor as they are immutable. Hence, we need to clone the existing request. We attach the headers to the cloned request and then pass that cloned request further in the pipeline.
  • We saw a demonstration of both the long and the short syntax used while configuring the injectors.
  • We learned that we explicitly need to specify the DI token – HTTP_INTERCEPTORS for configuring the injectors for the HTTP interceptors.
  • We learned that, although an injectable decorator is the recommended approach because of the tree-shaking provision, we cannot use it all the time for configuring the module injectors as it won’t allow us to specify the DI token explicitly.
  • We also learned the benefit of configuring the injectors using the NgModule decorator. It provides more configuration options compared to the Injectable decorator.
  • We learned that the injector needs to be configured with the multi providers for the HTTP interceptors.

Chapter 18 – Multi providers

  • In this chapter, we learned that it is possible to define more than one provider for a single DI token. This is referred to as a multi-provider.
  • We learned that if the multiple regular providers are defined for a single DI token, then one provider will replace the other based on the order.
  • We learned that if the multiple multi-providers are defined for a single DI token, then the injector will inject an array of services.
  • We learned that while defining a provider, the DI token and the actual services are not expected to be compatible. They can have a completely different structure.
  • We learned that we could not define both the regular provider and the multi-provider for a single DI token. Either all the providers should be regular, or all should be multi for a single DI token.
  • We learned that using the String or the Injection token with the multi-providers is recommended as the DI token instead of the Type token.
  • We learned about the Inject decorator that lets us manually tell Angular that the parameter has to be injected. It will be used in the case of the String and the Injection token.
  • We learned that the multi-provider could be very useful sometimes if we are creating a reusable service.

Chapter 19 – Compile-time configuration

  • We begin this chapter by understanding the need for configuration in the application.
  • We learned the difference between the compile-time and the run-time configuration. The compile-time configuration means the configuration will be done at the time of compilation, and the run-time configuration means it will be done at the time of deployment.
  • We learned about the environment.ts file and how it gets replaced with the environment.prod.ts file in the production mode.
  • We generated the non-production mode, and the production mode builds of our Angular application using the ng build and ng build --prod command, respectively.
  • We learned that in the non-production build, Angular CLI also generates the source map files; thus, we can directly debug the TypeScript files at run-time.
  • We learned that we wouldn’t get a separate vendor.js file in the production build as it is integrated into the main bundle.
  • We saw a demonstration of an Angular module called the lite-module that can be used as a development purpose web-server for our static files.

Chapter 20 – Run-time configuration

  • We learned that the assets folder located in the SRC folder of the Angular application would be copied to the final build.
  • We learned that we could hook into the Angular’s initialization process by configuring the root injector with a DI token provider – APP_ INITIALIZER.
  • We learned that we could provide a method as a value to the DI token using useFactory.
  • We spoke about the toPromise method of the observable class that creates a promise out of the observable.
  • We learned that while creating the providers, using the deps property, we can specify the current provider’s dependency. It is a must to explicitly define the dependency with useFactory.
  • We learned that in the case of useClass, we are not required to explicitly specify the dependent services, as the Injectable decorator does that for us. That is why, we have to attach an Injectable decorator to every service class, no matter what injector is configured for it.

Chapter 21 – Error Handling

This chapter was the last in Section 5, and thus lets us reach Station 10.

  • We had a detailed discussion on the Error handling in Angular.
  • We learned that we could attach a component-specific style to a component. For that, we will use the styleUrls parameter of the Component decorator.
  • We learned that Angular has a centralized exception handling already set in place. The default implementation prints the error messages to the console.
  • We learned that the default behavior could be overridden using a custom Angular service and injecting it into the Angular pipeline as a new error handler. For that, we have to configure the root injector for the DI token – ErrorHandler.
  • We learned that we have to implement the service with the ErrorHandler interface for creating a custom error handler service.
  • We learned about the zone.runOutsideAngular method that lets us execute the code outside the Angular’s execution context.
  • We learned about the zone.run method that lets us get back to the Angular’s execution context.

Section 6

CHAPTER 22

The Component-Oriented Style in Action

Introduction

This chapter is going to be a fascinating one. We will take up the previous project and improve it by actually following a component-oriented style. With this chapter, you will finish your journey to Station 11.

Component-oriented style

Component oriented style is a UI designing approach that will let us create our UI as a collection of reusable and composable web components.

Look at the following UI. What comes to your mind when you see it?

Figure 22.1

Isn’t it merely a composition of two labels, two text boxes, and two buttons?

What precisely are those labels, text boxes, and buttons? They are components.

Now, look at the following one. What do you see?

Figure 22.2

You may say – dropdown.

I won’t deny it. It’s indeed a dropdown.

  • But It can also be considered a combination of a textbox, a button, and a dynamic box displaying multiple items.
  • A button is placed using some CSS so that it looks like a part of the text box.
  • When that button is clicked, some code is executed, making a dynamic box appear at runtime, showing a couple of line items. When those line items are clicked, it gets displayed in the textbox.

What I meant to say is, a dropdown is a component, but it is a composition of other smaller elements or better referred to as components.

Based on whatever lab we have finished so far, I believe by now you must have a clear idea about the components.

A component represents a piece of the entire UI. We put those components together, form a giant component, and keep on doing it until the whole UI is done.

So far, in our application, we have seen a couple of components in action, such as LoginComponent, CustomerComponent, ErrorComponent and ErrorTestComponent, and so on.

Component oriented style and Angular

You may be amazed to learn that Angular does not coin a component-oriented style.

You can see a similar approach, followed by the other UI technologies such as Polymer, ReactJS, and so on.

It’s a standard approach/practice introduced with the emergence of HTML5.

This approach makes our code maintenance easy and lets multiple UI developers work parallelly.

A problem in the current application

Do you think we have followed the component-oriented style in the real manner in the current project that we have developed so far?

Well, partially yes and partially no.

We broke down the application into multiple components where each component had its role – Login, Customer, ErrorTest, and Error.

These top-level components will be identified based on the features of the project. Such components are referred to as the Feature components.

More features introduce more components, and those components will be accessed mostly using routing.

Once a feature component is identified and ready to be developed, the next step will be determining how each feature component will be designed. Creating one huge feature component won’t be a good idea as it makes the code unreadable and unmanageable. We should break it down into multiple smaller components.

In our example, the CustomerComponent is expected to be broken down into multiple smaller components. We haven’t done it, and that is the problem.

Container-Presentation pattern

When it comes to breaking down a feature component, the Container-Presentation pattern is widely used and proved.

In this approach, we will break our feature component into multiple components. One of them will be called a container component, and the others a presentation component.

Some people call it differently.

The container components will be referred to as the smart components. They will be the ones who will interact with the external APIS for retrieving and updating the data. They will be the ones responsible for the application state changes.

The presentation components are considered to be the dumb components. They are responsible for dealing with only one kind of functionality. They will take care of one part of the entire feature component logic.

They will rely on the container components for any interaction with the outside world, such as interacting with the external APIs, updating the application state, and so on.

You will understand it very well after the next demo.

Lab – Upgrade project to follow container-presentation pattern

To make it happen, we have to introduce two more new components – CustomerList and CustomerAdd.

  • Both the Components will be encapsulated inside CustomerComponent.
  • CustomerComponent will deal with CustomerService.

Next, we need to make everything work again step by step. Let’s start with the list data. If you remember, earlier we obtained it from the service.

Now, as per the container-presentation pattern, the presentation component should not deal with the Angular services. It should be purely meant for the presentation purposes. Interacting with an Angular service will be the container component’s task.

Then how does CustomerListComponent get the data?

We will pass it from the CustomerComponent to the CustomerListComponet, and for that, we will use the Input properties.

What were we doing earlier on AddNew?

We were invoking the setAddNew method of CustomerService.

Can we do the same now?

Yes, we can. Get the CustomerService instance injected into CustomerListComponent, and then invoke the method.

Should we do it?

No, because CustomerListComponent is a presentation component. The presentation component should not deal with any logic. It should ask the container component for such things.

The final question is how to invoke the container component function when the presentation component’s button is clicked.

That can be done by creating a custom output property in the CustomerListComponent, and for that, we will use an output decorator.

It has two steps. First, we need to refactor the existing Cancel method in the CustomerComponent.

Discussion – Continued

Revision on the Container-Presentation pattern

With the preceding step, we completed our demo on the Container-Presentation pattern.

Let’s quickly discuss how we shall decide what is to go where.

What part of our code should be considered in a container, and what should be the presentation?

All the operations related to the presentation will be a part of the Presentation component.

It includes sorting, paging, validating fields, formatting data, resetting the form, etc.

All the smart operations, such as the decision making, routing, and, most importantly, the coordination with the Angular service, will be a part of the Container component.

Pending issues

Before we end this chapter, let’s solve two pending issues in the lab – autofocus in the first control and the default-enter. Let’s start with autofocus.

If you are thinking about using the autofocus attribute in HTML, you will be disappointed.

The HTML autofocus attribute sets focus on the element when the page is loaded for the first time.

Try it out quickly:

  • Set the autofocus attribute on the firstName textbox and execute the application.
  • Click on AddNew, you will find the focus on the firstName textbox.
  • Click on Cancel, and then click on AddNew again. Unfortunately, you won’t find the focus set back.

To solve this problem, we will use the ViewChild decorator and the template reference variable. Using these two, we can get the view element access in the component class.

The next question is, when will we set the focus? We have to set the focus as soon as the component is loaded, and the control is ready to focus.

Let’s try with the constructor.

Lab – Continued

Let’s attach a template reference variable to the firstname textbox.

  1.    <input #firstName class=”form-control”
  2. [ngClass]=”{‘is-valid’:F.valid,’is-invalid’:F.invalid}”
  3. type=”text” name=”FName”[(ngModel)]=”this.FirstName” required
  4. minlength=”3” #F=”ngModel”>

In the preceding code, you can notice a template reference variable firstname is attached to the textbox.

Step 29 – Create a reference to control in the Component class

Open the CustomerAddComponent class and create a variable FirstNameControl of the type ElementRef as follows:

  1. ……
  2. import {Component, ElementRef, EventEmitter, Output, ViewChild}
  3. from ‘@angular/core’;
  4. ……
  5. export class CustomerAddComponent{
  6. ……
  7.    @ViewChild(“firstName”) FirstNameControl: ElementRef;
  8. ……

Step 30 – Set focus

Set the focus using the following code in the constructor:

  1. export class CustomerAddComponent implements AfterViewInit  {
  2. ……
  3.    constructor(){
  4.      this.FirstNameControl.nativeElement.focus();
  5.   }
  6. ……

Step 31 – Check the output

Open the application and click on AddNew. You will land on the error page. To check the error, you have to check the local storage.

Figure 22.7

Discussion – Continued

Error handler issue

Is it annoying to check the errors like this?

Whenever there is an error, you will get redirected to an error page. Then, you have to find out the error in the local storage.

That may be an ideal way in the production environment, but in the development environment, I think the default approach makes more sense where the red error gets displayed in the console.

Is there a better way? Yes, there is. Open your AppErrorHandler and add the following block of code at the beginning of the handleError function:

  1.    if(!environment.production){
  2.        throw error;
  3.     }

The complete handleError function looks like the following:

  1. ……
  2. import {Router} from ‘@angular/router’;
  3. import {environment} from ‘src/environments/environment’;
  4.  
  5. @Injectable()
  6. export class AppErrorsHandler implements ErrorHandler {
  7. ……
  8.    handleError(error: Error | HttpErrorResponse) {
  9.      if(!environment.production){
  10.        alert(‘Run-time error occured. Kindly check developer tools’)
  11.        throw error;
  12.     }
  13.      if (error instanceof HttpResponseBase) {
  14.        this.HandleServerSideError(error); // Indicates its a server side error
  15.     } else {
  16.        this.HandleClientSideError(error); // Indicates its a client side error
  17.     }
  18.   }
  19. ……

After this change, your custom error handler comes to the picture only if the current environment is a production environment.

How to solve the focus issue?

Now the question is, how to tackle the focus issue? Writing the logic insider constructor is not working. A constructor is invoked when the instance of CustomerAddComponent got created. The textbox does not even exist at that moment.

One solution is the Angular life cycle events. Angular lets us hook into the Angular execution process by exposing a lot of life cycle methods. We can put our custom logic into those methods and do custom things.

One such life cycle method is ngOnInit. It executes once the component is initialized.

Let’s try it out.

Lab – Continued

Step 32 – Implement ngOnInit and add focus logic

For that, implement CustomerAddComponent with OnInit interface, which will force us to define the ngOnInit method. In ngOnInit, set the focus on the firstName textbox.

  1. import {Component, ElementRef, EventEmitter, OnInit, Output, ViewChild}
  2. from ‘@angular/core’;
  3. ……
  4. @Component({
  5.    selector: ‘customer-add’,
  6.    templateUrl: ‘./customer-add.component.html’
  7. })
  8. export class CustomerAddComponent implements OnInit  {
  9.    ……
  10.    @ViewChild(“firstName”) FirstNameControl: ElementRef;
  11.    ngOnInit(){
  12.      this.FirstNameControl.nativeElement.focus();
  13.   }
  14. ……

Step 33 – Check the output

Unfortunately, this won’t work either.

Discussion – Continued

Unfortunately, ngOnInit was not helpful. It gets invoked once the component is initialized. At this point, the controls are not rendered, hence, this.FirsNameControl will be undefined.

Note: Kindly understand that the constructor component was not even initialized, whereas, during ngOnInt, it is initialized but not rendered.

We have a perfect life cycle method for this situation – ngAfterViewInit. It is an ideal candidate for the logic that needs access over the rendered controls.

Let’s use the same.

Lab – Continued

Step 34 – Implement ngAfterViewInit

Implement CustomerAddComponent with AfterViewInit interface and then define the ngAfterViewInit method as follows:

  1. import {AfterViewInit, Component, ElementRef, EventEmitter,
  2. Output, ViewChild} from ‘@angular/core’;
  3. ……
  4. export class CustomerAddComponent implements AfterViewInit  {
  5. …….
  6.    @ViewChild(“firstName”) FirstNameControl: ElementRef;

Step 35 – Check the output

Finally, you will find it working. You will notice that the firstName textbox will have the focus every time CustomerAddNewComponent is accessed.

Discussion – Continued

So, with the preceding step, we were successful with the focus requirement. Next, let’s solve the default enter issue.

If you remember, previously, we achieved it by putting the entire section inside a form tag and changing the regular button with a submit button.

Replace the containerdiv element in the CustomerAddComponent with the form tag and the regular button to submit the button as follows:

  1.    <form class=”card” #myForm=”ngForm”>
  2.      <h5 class=”card-header”>Add New Customer</h5>
  3. ……

Enter some values in both the text boxes and just press enter. It will trigger the Save function automatically, and we will have achieved our target.

Discussion – Continued

Though everything looks fantastic, there is something different compared to previous time. Did you notice it?

The ngForm directive was explicitly attached to the div tag before.

Did you notice that we have not attached the ngFormdirective explicitly to our form tag? Then, how come everything is working?

Well, in the template-driven forms, the ngFrom directive gets automatically attached to the form elements—no need to do it explicitly.

That is the reason why we removed it when we changed div to form.

Summary

We have now completed our journey to Station 11. Let’s quickly revise what we have learned in this chapter:

  • We discussed a new UI development approach in the modern world – component-oriented style. It is a UI designing approach that will let us create our UI as a composition of multiple smaller and reusable components.
  • We learned that Angular is not the pioneer of the component-oriented approach. It is just following it. The other technologies, like react and polymer, follow a similar process.
  • We learned that this approach makes our code maintenance easy and lets multiple UI developers work parallelly.
  • We spoke about the components that represent the application’s main components and are mostly accessed via routing.
  • We learned that sometimes it is considered to break down a feature component into smaller components to make the code readable and manageable. The container-presentation pattern is one of the commonly followed patterns in industry for this purpose.
  • We had a quick discussion on the difference between the container and the presentation components. The container component is usually the smart one, whereas the presentation components are termed as the dumb components and they deal with the UI presentation.
  • We created the custom input property for passing the data from the outer component to the inner component.
  • We created the custom output property for raising even from the inner component that can be handled in the outer component.
  • We revisited the Viewchild decorator and template reference variable and learned to reference the component class’s view element.
  • We learned about using the environment again in this chapter. We made our error handler code behave differently for the different environments (dev and production).
  • We revisited ngOnInit and learned how it is best suited for the initialization logic.
  • We learned about the ngAfterViewInit life cycle, a perfect candidate for logic that needs access over the rendered controls.
  • We learned that we are not required to explicitly assign the ngForm directive to the form tag in the template-driven forms.

Lab 7 – Angular Routing

Step 1 – Rename application

Rename the application to lab7-ng from lab6-ng.

Step 2 – Create more components for the demo

We require some more components for this demo. Create a folder Supplier and Product inside the app folder and then create the respective components inside.

  1. import {Component} from ‘@angular/core’;
  2.  
  3. @Component({
  4.    selector: ‘supplier’,
  5.    template: ‘<h1>Welcome to supplier</h1>’
  6. })

  9.    constructor() {}

  6. })
  8. export class ProductComponent {
  9.    constructor() {}
  10. }

As you can see, this time, we have a template instead of templateURL.

Using a template, we can specify the component HTML inline instead of having it in a separate HTML file.

  1. ……
  2. import {ProductComponent} from ‘./Product/product.component’;
  3. ……
  4. import {SupplierComponent} from ‘./Supplier/supplier.component’;
  5. @NgModule({
  6.    declarations: [AppComponent, LoginComponent,
  7.      CustomerComponent, ErrorTestComponent, ErrorComponent,
  8.      CustomerAddComponent, CustomerListComponent,
  9.      ProductComponent, SupplierComponent
  10.   ],
  11. ……
  12.    bootstrap: [AppComponent],
  13. })
  14. export class AppModule {}

Don’t forget to add them to AppModule.

Step 3 – Prepare to route

Next, open app.routes.ts and configure the route for both of the preceding components as follows:

  1. ……
  2. import {ProductComponent} from ‘../Product/product.component’;
  3. import {SupplierComponent} from ‘../Supplier/supplier.component’;
  4.  
  5. export const AppRoutes: Routes = [
  6.    {path: ‘login’, component: LoginComponent},
  7.    {path: ‘customer’, component: CustomerComponent, canActivate: [AuthGuard]},
  8.    {path: ‘supplier’, component: SupplierComponent, canActivate: [AuthGuard]},
  9.    {path: ‘product’, component: ProductComponent, canActivate: [AuthGuard]},
  10.    {path: ‘error-test’, component: ErrorTestComponent},
  11.    {path: ‘error’, component: ErrorComponent},
  12.    {path: ‘’, redirectTo: ‘login’, pathMatch: ‘full’},
  13.    {path: ‘**’, redirectTo: ‘customer’, pathMatch: ‘full’},
  14. ];

Discussion – Continued

Now, we have something interesting. We have the following three problems to address:

  1. We want to create a menu for navigating between the preceding components.

    The question is, in which component will we add the menu?

    If we add it to the AppComponent, then it will be visible even on the login screen.

    Explicitly doing it in each component will not be feasible as it will violate the DRY principle. (Don’t repeat yourself – once the code is written, don’t repeat it).

  2. Secondly, check the preceding route configuration code. Have you noticed the AuthGuard attached to each route? Again, that is a violation of the DRY principle. It is our second problem.
  3. Finally, in one of our previous chapters, we added logged in user’s name and logout link in the customer component. As an application, it has to be present on every page. That is the third problem.

The solution for all the three problems is nested routes.

We will introduce another component – AuthComponent, the parent component for the menus, the user’s name, the logout link, and all the other authorize-required-components.

Lab – Continued

Step 4 – Create AuthComponent

Create a new folder in the app folder called Auth and then create a new component called AuthComponent as follows:

  1. import {Component} from ‘@angular/core’;
  2. import {AuthenticationService} from ‘../Services/authentication.service’;
  3. import * as jwt_decode from ‘jwt-decode’;
  4. @Component({
  5.    selector: ‘auth-root’,
  6.    templateUrl: ‘./auth.component.html’
  7. })
  8. export class AuthComponent {
  9.    LoginUserFirstName = ‘DummyFName’;
  10.  
  11.    constructor(private authenticationService: AuthenticationService) {
  12.        const decodedToken = jwt_decode(localStorage.token);
  13.        this.LoginUserFirstName = decodedToken.firstName;
  14.   }
  15.    logout() {
  16.      this.authenticationService.logout();
  17.   }
  18. }

As you can see, the username and the logout code from CustomerComponent is shifted to AuthComponent.

(Please ensure that the corresponding code is removed from CustomerComponent as it is not relevant anymore.)

The template file should look like the following:

  1. <nav class=”navbar navbar-expand navbar-dark bg-dark”>
  2.    <div class=”collapse navbar-collapse” id=”navbarSupportedContent”>
  3.      <ul class=”navbar-nav mr-auto”>
  4.        <li class=”nav-item “>
  5.          <a class=”nav-link” href=”/customer”>Customer</a>
  6.        </li>
  7.        <li class=”nav-item “>
  8.          <a class=”nav-link” href=”/supplier”>Supplier</a>

Although everything is working as per the expectation, there is one big problem in the preceding lab, that is, eager loading.
